info.bio:
John Denver (Roswell, Nuevo México, 31 de diciembre de 1943 - Pacific Grove, California, 12 de octubre de 1997), nacido como Henry John Deutschendorf, Jr. en Roswell, Nuevo México. Murió con 53 años de edad en la costa de Monterey, California cuando pilotaba un Rutan Long-EZ, un avión experimental de fibra de vidrio.
Fue tal vez el principal exponente de la música country de EEUU. Dedicó su vida a cantarle a la naturaleza, las relaciones y los valores humanos y a la preservacion de la vida.

scenes.name: El PMRC y las audiencias del Senado
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: El Parents Music Resource Center, fundado por esposas de políticos de Washington, lleva en 1985 la «música obscena» al Senado de Estados Unidos en las audiencias sobre el etiquetado de discos. Allí el musicólogo Joe Stuessy, asesor del PMRC, declara que el heavy actual es categóricamente distinto de toda música popular anterior porque contiene odio, y el senador Albert Gore pregunta por la tendencia a la violencia explícita, el sexo y el sadomasoquismo «en el área del heavy metal». Para Weinstein es el ejemplo de cómo el género se convierte en asunto público sin que nadie sepa de qué está hablando.

scenes.name: Cantautores de los setenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: James Taylor se convierte, misteriosamente, en el prototipo del cantautor de los setenta; Carole King, Carly Simon y Don McLean, sobrevalorados. Las innovaciones llegan del oeste: Randy Newman y sus viñetas urbanas con fusión de estilos populares, Shawn Phillips, J.J. Cale y su estilo «laid-back», Gram Parsons, Emmylou Harris, Roger McGuinn, Jackson Browne (Late For The Sky) y, sobre todo, Tom Waits, discípulo de Beefheart y cronista de marginados (Swordfishtrombones, Rain Dogs). Excéntricos como Todd Rundgren y Annette Peacock; en Gran Bretaña, Peter Hammill, Anthony Moore, Richard Thompson, Robert Calvert, John Cale, Kevin Coyne, Elton John y los ex Beatles. El realismo de Bruce Springsteen, verdadero heredero de Woody Guthrie y del blues, y la escuela italiana de cantautores (De André, Guccini, Battisti, Sorrenti).

podcast.title: Successful Plagiarism Lawsuit Against New Order (1990)
podcast.body: In 1990, John Denver successfully sued New Order for plagiarism, winning the case against them for similarities between his song "Leaving on a Jet Plane" (a 1969 number one hit for Peter, Paul and Mary) and New Order's 1990 song "Run." "In 1990, John Denver, this cute little folk singer who looked like a muffet, nailed New Order with a plagiarism suit and won."

podcast.title: "The Great Outdoors" Persona
podcast.body: John Denver's persona as a pop star was significantly defined by his "uncool" interest in "The Great Outdoors," frequently singing about nature and particularly the majesty of the Colorado mountains, the state from which he adopted his stage name. His brand was characterized by wide-eyed earnestness. "What defined John Denver as a pop star was his most uncool interest, The Great Outdoors."

podcast.title: Birth and Upbringing
podcast.body: Born in 1943 in Roswell, New Mexico, John Denver (Henry John Deutschendorf Jr.) was the son of Henry John Deutschendorf Sr., a decorated Air Force captain. His childhood involved frequent relocations across the South and Southwestern United States due to his father's military transfers. "Born in 1943 in Roswell, New Mexico to Henry John Doichendorf Sr., a decorated captain in the Air Force, Doichendorf Jr. grew up all over the South and Southwestern United States, as his dad was transferred from base to base."

podcast.body: Denver's success, alongside Olivia Newton-John's, generated controversy within the country establishment, with some artists bristling at these "outsiders" dominating their charts and winning prizes over long-established country acts. "Some artists in the country establishment bristle that these outsiders coming into the genre, dominating their charts, and even winning prizes over acts that had been recording country music for decades."

podcast.title: FCC Ban of "Rocky Mountain High"
podcast.body: The lyric "and everybody's high" in "Rocky Mountain High" caused the song to be briefly banned by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for allegedly celebrating drug abuse. John Denver intended the lyric to mean "high on life" and the natural wonders of Colorado, and he never forgot this act of censorship, decrying it later in his career. "But everybody's high briefly got the song banned by the Federal Communications Commission as celebrating drug abuse, an act of censorship that Denver never forgot and would decry later in his career."

concerts.title: The Midnight Special Pilot (1972)
concerts.body: John Denver hosted the 90-minute pilot of *The Midnight Special* in August 1972, which focused on encouraging young people to vote. During the show, he discussed voter registration with Cass Elliott and performed "Leaving on a Jet Plane" with her. "The host was John Denver who was writing this wave of success from Take Me Home Country Roads and was about to have even more success with Rocky Mountain High."

xref.title: Nurturing Musical Environment
xref.body: The Kiszka brothers were raised in a "musically nurturing environment" that extended beyond just music to include film and literature. They were surrounded by traditional music, including early American blues artists like Elmore James, Willie Dixon, Robert Johnson, Muddy Waters, and Howlin' Wolf, as well as folk artists like Arlo Guthrie, Bob Dylan, Joni Mitchell, and John Denver, primarily from their parents' vinyl collection. "we were kind of raised in a musically nurturing environment where it wasn't necessarily just music, but there was a lot of film and a lot of literature. And we had a lot of traditional music, you know, lying around."
